sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The two-pointer pattern tracks two positions whose movement removes impossible candidates. Common forms move inward from both ends or move at different speeds through one sequence.

For pair sum in ascending data, add the end values. A small sum requires moving the left pointer right; a large sum requires moving the right pointer left.

For example, with `[1,3,4,7,10]` and target `11`, `1+10` succeeds immediately. For target `10`, `1+10` is too large, so moving the right pointer removes `10` from consideration.

The pattern is not automatically O(n) unless each pointer moves only one direction a bounded number of times. Sorting first also adds O(n log n) time and may lose original indexes.

Two pointers can replace a nested pair loop when ordering or another invariant proves that one movement discards a whole group of candidates safely.

sections.title: The core model: the two-pointer pattern
sections.content:
the two-pointer pattern is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

The pattern gains speed by exploiting structure. Instead of trying every pair, one comparison rules out many pairs at once. In a sorted pair-sum search, if the smallest remaining value plus the largest is too small, pairing that same smallest value with anything else cannot reach the target.

sections.title: the two-pointer pattern example
the two-pointer pattern at a glance
sections.content:
| State | Meaning | Safe move |
|---|---|---|
| Sum below target | Left value is too small with largest remaining | `left++` |
| Sum above target | Right value is too large with smallest remaining | `right--` |
| Sum equals target | Pair found | Return |

sections.title: The practical decision: the two-pointer pattern
sections.content:
The useful question is not whether the two-pointer pattern can be used, but which requirement makes it the clearest and safest fit. That decision includes its cost and its failure boundary.

Useful signals include sorted data, symmetric comparison, in-place compaction, and slow/fast traversal. Without such a monotonic relationship, a map or nested search may be more appropriate. Sorting can create the relationship, but its cost and effect on indexes must be included.

sections.title: Why the failure happens: the two-pointer pattern
sections.content:
Failures around the two-pointer pattern usually come from one incorrect assumption about ownership, state, ordering, or lifetime. Finding that assumption is more useful than adding a defensive line at random.

Every pointer update needs a sentence explaining what has been eliminated. If no such sentence is true, the algorithm may skip candidates. Progress is the second proof: at least one pointer must move toward termination on every non-returning iteration.

sections.title: The important trade-off: the two-pointer pattern
sections.content:
the two-pointer pattern and nested pair checking solve related problems, but they expose different guarantees. The best choice follows from the guarantee the program actually needs.

A sliding window also uses two indexes, but the indexes describe a whole contiguous segment whose sum, count, or validity is updated incrementally. Opposite-end two pointers usually compare a pair. Recognising which state matters prevents forcing one template onto a different problem.

sections.title: A reliable diagnosis: the two-pointer pattern
sections.content:
A good investigation traces the first point where the real state differs from the expected state. With the two-pointer pattern, that means observing the relevant input, transition, and result rather than guessing from the final symptom.

A dry-run table is more useful than a final output because it records the invariant in motion. Include left and right indexes, their values, the derived sum, and the reason for the move. At exit, explain whether a match was found or the candidate interval became empty.
